unit: W1-9 429 contract on both classes (PR #152, merge a4e7b08b), lockout path focus

defects.location: app/services/auth_service.py track_failed_login / check_account_locked (origin/main 2ec8131e, ~lines 776-805)
defects.claim: The lockout counter is armed non-atomically: INCR, then EXPIRE only when count == 1. If that one EXPIRE never lands (an exception or timeout, or an INCR that ran on the server but timed out on the client), the key has no TTL for good. Five failed logins over ANY span of time then lock the account permanently. check_account_locked returns retry_after = max(ttl=-1, 0) = 0, so the new W1-9 handler sends the 429 with no Retry-After and no retry_after_seconds.
defects.why_it_matters: The lock can never lift. clear_failed_logins only runs after a successful login, PUT /email or PUT /password, and the lockout check blocks all three first. Password reset does not clear the counter either. The user is locked out with no window and no self-service way out until someone deletes the Redis key by hand. The storage is Upstash REST: INCR and EXPIRE are two HTTP round-trips, the bounded transport has rest_retries=0, and exceptions are swallowed, so one transient failure is enough. The counter is in Redis, keyed per email hash. It is shared across processes and survives a redeploy, which makes the stuck key permanent. If redis_client is None, lockout fails open entirely.
defects.proposed_fix_unit: Files: app/services/auth_service.py plus a new tests/test_lockout_ttl_integrity.py. Change: make arming atomic. Either SET key 0 EX LOCKOUT_WINDOW_SECONDS NX followed by INCR, or a pipeline/MULTI, confirming what upstash-redis 1.7.0 supports on the pinned venv. As defence in depth, have check_account_locked (and track_failed_login) re-arm expire(key, LOCKOUT_WINDOW_SECONDS) whenever ttl == -1. Red test: an in-memory FakeRedis whose expire() raises TimeoutError on its first call. Drive POST /auth/login 7 times with login_user mocked to fail, log_audit_event stubbed, and limiter.reset() between calls. Today: [401 x5, 429 ACCOUNT_LOCKED x2, no Retry-After], key ttl=-1, count=5, forever (measured). After the fix: the key carries a positive TTL, and every locked 429 carries Retry-After == retry_after_seconds > 0.

defects.location: app/services/auth_service.py:788 (retry_after = max(ttl, 0)) vs app/middleware/error_handler.py:_retry_after_seconds (int(1 + reset - now))
defects.claim: The two 429 producers share a field name but round differently. The slowapi path rounds UP (+1, deliberately, so the client never comes back early). The lockout path ships Redis TTL, which Redis rounds to the NEAREST second, so it can be up to ~0.5 s short. A client that returns exactly at Retry-After can therefore hit a still-locked key whose TTL now reads 0, or -2 if the key expired between the GET and the TTL, and get a 429 ACCOUNT_LOCKED with no window. The -2 case reports 'locked' although the lock has already lifted.
defects.why_it_matters: The client half (W3-14) is told to read retry_after_seconds and nothing else. A client that honours the lockout value exactly can land in a second 429 with no window, which is the hammer-or-give-up behaviour W1-9 was meant to end.
defects.proposed_fix_unit: Files: app/services/auth_service.py. In check_account_locked, use PTTL and ceil(ms/1000) + 1, or TTL + 1 when ttl > 0. When ttl <= 0 and the GET said locked, treat -2 as unlocked, and treat -1 by re-arming as in the first defect. Red test: FakeRedis with get='5' and ttl in {-2, 0}, POST /auth/login. Measured today: 429 ACCOUNT_LOCKED with no Retry-After for ttl -2, -1 and 0. For -2 it should be allowed through to login. What I ran: the handler/route half (the no-window 429 for ttl -2/-1/0). The Redis rounding half is from Redis's ttlGenericCommand ((ms+500)/1000), not executed here because there is no Redis offline.

summary: I re-ran the W1-9 file on the pinned venv (17 passed) and probed both 429 producers through the real app in a scratch worktree, which is now removed; the shared trees were never touched. The diff itself holds up. The slowapi 429 emits Retry-After and retry_after_seconds from one value on the pinned 0.1.10. Epoch values and already-elapsed windows are refused. When the window cannot be read, the handler serves the old 429. Successful responses carry no X-RateLimit-* headers, and that pin is real. The SSE route's 429 is JSON with the header, sent before the stream starts. With no window, the response is byte-identical to before. The lockout path it surfaced is not sound. (1) Arming the lock is non-atomic: INCR, then EXPIRE only when the count is 1, over Upstash REST, with errors swallowed. One failed EXPIRE leaves a TTL-less key, and five failed logins at any time afterwards lock the account permanently with no Retry-After and no way out. Reproduced with a fake Redis: [401 x5, 429 x2], ttl -1. (2) The slowapi path rounds up; the lockout TTL rounds to nearest; and ttl -2/-1/0 all produce a windowless ACCOUNT_LOCKED 429 (the handler half reproduced; the Redis rounding comes from Redis source, not a run). (3) With ENABLE_DEFAULT_RATE_LIMITS on, SlowAPIMiddleware on the pinned 0.1.10 discards our async handler: /health 429s with slowapi's bare body. Swapping in SlowAPIASGIMiddleware fixes it (measured: full envelope, Retry-After: 60). The CLAUDE.md flag row still lacks this precondition. (4) Mutation checks found two unpinned claims: the +1 round-up (removing it left 17/17 green) and the retry_after wiring on PUT /email and /password (removing it left 23 green). The PR body's 'retry_after=300' is also wrong: the value is the Redis TTL, up to 900.

defects.claim: The PR says it closed the failure where the metric 'can silently read 0 forever'. It did not. Three mutants of the live wiring each leave all 10 tests in the file green. (A) /health returns the literal {"loop_lag_ms": 0.0, "loop_lag_max_ms": 0.0} in place of **loop_lag_snapshot(). (B) The heartbeat calls record_loop_lag_tick(LOOP_LAG_INTERVAL_SECONDS), which is always 0 lag, in place of now - previous. (C) The heartbeat drops `previous = now`, so the reported lag grows by 1000 ms every tick forever. The new wiring pin (test_heartbeat_actually_calls_the_recorder) only checks that the recorder was called with some value >= 0, never that the value is the measured elapsed time. And no test records a tick and then reads it back through GET /health.
defects.why_it_matters: The only named consumer of this signal is the W5 STEP-0 canary gate: CLAUDE.md, the full review's activation order, and the session log all say to watch loop_lag through every flag flip. With mutant A or B, /health reports 0 lag while the loop is wedged, which reads as 'safe to proceed'. That is exactly the failure the PR body says was pinned. With mutant C the max climbs without bound, so a canary would be rolled back for no reason. The code on main is correct today. What is missing is protection against a regression.
defects.proposed_fix_unit: Tests only, in tests/test_health_loop_lag.py. (1) test_health_reflects_recorded_lag: call app_main.record_loop_lag_tick(LOOP_LAG_INTERVAL_SECONDS + 0.7), then GET /health through TestClient(app) without a lifespan block, so the heartbeat cannot overwrite it. Assert loop_lag_ms is about 700 and loop_lag_max_ms >= 700. This kills mutant A. (2) Tighten test_heartbeat_actually_calls_the_recorder: set LOOP_LAG_INTERVAL_SECONDS=0.01, collect 3 or more elapsed values, and use loop.call_later to schedule time.sleep(0.2) right after the first tick. Assert that some elapsed value is >= 0.15 (kills B, constant elapsed) and that every value is < 0.5 (kills C, which accumulates 0.01, 0.02, ... and then about 0.2 plus the total so far). Better still, drive it with a fake loop.time sequence to avoid wall-clock flake. Red check: apply mutants A, B and C from a byte snapshot and confirm each new test goes red, then restore with a sha256 check.

defects.location: app/main.py:197-210 (record_loop_lag_tick / _loop_lag_max_ms), app/main.py:183-185 comment ('rolling MAX'), CLAUDE.md:524 and CONTEXT_SESSION_LOG.md:60 ('watch it climb WITHIN that process')
defects.claim: loop_lag_max_ms is not a rolling max. It is a high-water mark that never decays, and it is sampled by a single 1 s sleep-overshoot timer. Both properties were measured by running the merged heartbeat source. (a) Saturation: after one 11 s stall, 3,600 healthy ticks, then a NEW 4 s stall followed by one healthy tick, /health reads {loop_lag_ms: 0.0, loop_lag_max_ms: 11000.0}. The new stall is invisible to both numbers. (b) Sub-second blindness: a 900 ms blocking call that starts 50 ms after the heartbeat goes to sleep is reported as 15 ms, the Windows timer floor. A 400 ms block is reported as 15 ms. Only a block that straddles the deadline is seen (900 ms at phase 0.95 s reports 860 ms). Any single stall is under-reported by up to one full interval, and a stall under 1 s can be missed entirely. The docs record the prod idle floor climbing from 1-3 ms right after a deploy to 286 ms over one process lifetime, so the high-water mark fills with noise, and after that only a record-breaking event moves it.
defects.why_it_matters: W5 STEP 0 is supposed to watch this number through ENABLE_OFFLOOP_DNS_RESOLVE and ENABLE_PRICE_PARSE_OFFLOAD. The second flag exists to remove sub-second on-loop CPU, which is exactly what a 1 s overshoot sampler under-reports. A monotone max cannot show a flip making things better, and it cannot show a second, smaller regression after the first spike. The runbook's instruction to 'watch it climb within the process' is therefore weaker than it reads. It resets only when the process restarts (proven: a fresh process reads 0.0/0.0, and the docs record prod reading 285.99 ms before a deploy and 1.0 ms after), so a canary can read only 'the worst tick since boot'.
defects.proposed_fix_unit: app/main.py only, additive, and /health stays a dict read. Keep loop_lag_ms and loop_lag_max_ms exactly as they are. Add three things: (1) loop_lag_max_60s_ms, the max over a 60-slot ring of per-tick values, updated in record_loop_lag_tick in O(1) amortized time, or bucketed per 10 s; (2) loop_lag_stalls_over_250ms, a monotone count of ticks whose lag exceeded 250 ms, so a canary compares rates instead of a saturating max; (3) loop_lag_max_at, the loop.time or wall-clock timestamp of the high-water mark. Optionally drop LOOP_LAG_INTERVAL_SECONDS to 0.25 so sub-second stalls are seen. The cost stays negligible: 5.2 s idle measured 0.0 ms of CPU at 1 s, and at 4 Hz it is still trivial. Correct the 'rolling MAX' comment to 'high-water mark since process start'. Red tests: feed the recorder 11 s, then 60 healthy ticks, then 4 s, and assert loop_lag_max_60s_ms is about 3000 while loop_lag_max_ms stays 11000; assert the stall counter increments on each tick over 250 ms. Update the W5 runbook to read the windowed max and the stall count.

defects.location: tests/test_start_command.py (module docstring, _tokens docstring, test_limit_concurrency_is_a_real_uvicorn_option_on_this_build); railway.json:7; Procfile:1
defects.claim: The shell-expansion proof exists only as prose in a docstring. The tests pin the byte string (mutant F, unquoting both files, is correctly killed), but nothing executes it. I re-derived it for the current command, which now also carries `exec` and --timeout-graceful-shutdown from W1-6, through both Git-bash sh and /usr/bin/dash with an argv stub: unset or empty gives [512]; 250 gives [250]; '1 --workers 4' and '$(id)' each arrive as ONE inert argument. On the pinned uvicorn 0.52.4 CLI, 512 and 250 are accepted, while '1 --workers 4' and the literal '${UVICORN_LIMIT_CONCURRENCY:-512}' exit 2 as 'not a valid integer', so a literal reaching uvicorn is confirmed to be a boot failure. Four problems remain. (i) The docstring is stale: it still says '100 is chosen against measured traffic' and 'Neither command contains quoting today, and neither should'. (ii) The version-drift guard checks uvicorn.config.Config.__init__, not the CLI option. A CLI rename that kept the Config kwarg would pass it and still crash-loop. (iii) uvicorn's click command carries context_settings auto_envvar_prefix='UVICORN', so UVICORN_LIMIT_CONCURRENCY is ALSO read natively. Measured: with no flag and the env set to 77, uvicorn uses limit 77. UVICORN_WORKERS=4 also reconfigures the merged command natively. So the PR's injection rationale for the quotes is moot: anyone who can set env vars can already set any uvicorn option. The quotes are still correct. (iv) 0 and -5 are accepted. A limit of 0 sheds every request including /health (len(connections) >= 0), so an operator using the common '0 = unlimited' convention would fail the deploy healthcheck.

The protection is a byte pin plus a one-off manual proof, and the reasoning recorded next to it is partly wrong, so the next editor gets misleading guidance. activation_gate: No flag. This has been live since 8eaa0d45. Every deploy boots with --limit-concurrency set from UVICORN_LIMIT_CONCURRENCY, defaulting to 512, and /health carries loop_lag_ms and loop_lag_max_ms. The docs say it is live in production (prod /health 3.0 ms at 8eaa0d45, and 285.99 then 1.0 ms across the 08167de1 deploy); I did not re-verify prod because the network was out of scope. On the evidence it is safe: expansion is proven under sh and dash, the pinned uvicorn 0.52.4 accepts the value, the heartbeat costs about 0 CPU and cannot block, and /health stays a dict read. Two operational gates follow. (1) Before any W5 STEP-0 canary is judged on this signal, land the wiring pins (defect 1) and the windowed max plus stall counter (defect 2). As shipped, the max saturates on the first big stall and under-reports stalls under 1 s, so it cannot show a flip's effect on sub-second on-loop CPU (ENABLE_PRICE_PARSE_OFFLOAD). Until then, a canary must read the max only within one process lifetime, and a lack of climb is not evidence of improvement. (2) Before anyone lowers UVICORN_LIMIT_CONCURRENCY: shed responses are a bare 503 from the server layer (measured in-process against the real app.main:app on both httptools and h11: text/plain 'Service Unavailable', only content-type, content-length and connection: close; no envelope, no X-Request-ID, no security headers). /health itself is shed. The gate counts open connections, so in the probe, 3 connections against a limit of 2 shed the FIRST request too. The mobile client maps a bare 503 to TIMEOUT copy with no automatic retry, which is a graceful outcome. The only telemetry is uvicorn's WARNING 'Exceeded concurrency limit.' log line, so set up a log alert on it before tuning. Never set the value to 0 or a negative number: uvicorn accepts both, and 0 sheds everything, including the deploy healthcheck.

unit: W1-4 client half: logout sends the stored refresh_token (PR #140, merge ece0fbbe; reviewed at origin/main 2ec8131e)

defects.location: SmartCompareApp/src/services/authService.ts:245-266 (logout reads the stored access token and never refreshes it) + SmartCompareApp/src/services/api.ts:214 (/auth/logout is excluded from the 401 refresh-retry) + app/api/auth_routes.py:652-656 (Depends(get_current_user) runs before logout_user)
defects.claim: Upstream revocation is skipped without any signal whenever logout carries an expired access token. That includes logging out while a refresh is still in flight, a Profile screen left open for more than an hour and then resumed, and a boot refresh that failed on a network blip. The server returns 401 from get_current_user before logout_user runs. The client interceptor skips refresh for /auth/logout, and logout() does not wait for or start a refresh, so no retry happens. The in-flight refresh then finishes on the server and rotates RT1 to RT2. The P-A3 epoch guard discards RT2 on the phone, so RT2 stays valid upstream and nothing revokes it. The CLAUDE.md flag row says the expired path is common and still revokes 'via that rotation plus the sign_out on the NEW session'. That path cannot be reached through the route: set_session's expired branch only runs when logout_user is called directly.
defects.why_it_matters: The unit exists to make logout revoke upstream. Its own docs call the expired-token case common, and there the flag does nothing and the only record is the 1 h Redis blacklist of an access token that has already expired. The local clear still happens (verified), so users see no problem. What fails is the security claim.
defects.proposed_fix_unit: Client (SmartCompareApp/src/services/api.ts + authService.ts): export a read-only `getInFlightRefresh(): Promise<RefreshResult> | null` from api.ts. At the top of logout(), if a refresh is in flight, await it (swallow errors), then read the access and refresh tokens. If the access token's `exp` has passed (decode the JWT payload without verifying it), call getOrStartRefresh() first and use the new pair. Send exactly one POST with no retry loop, and keep clearSession in `finally`. Server alternative, which also covers the builds already on phones: let /auth/logout accept a presented but expired Bearer when the flag is on and a refresh_token is in the body. Parse the Bearer without verifying it and let logout_user's set_session expired branch rotate and sign out. Red tests: (1) a client jest test in which refreshSession's POST is a pending deferred and logout() is called concurrently. Today the logout POST carries 'Bearer AT1-expired' and {refresh_token:'RT1'}, and my scratch test asserting that passes. After the fix it must carry AT2/RT2, or come after the refresh settles. (2) A backend test: POST /api/v1/auth/logout with an expired Bearer, a refresh_token body and the flag ON. Measured today: 401 and logout_user called 0 times. After the fix it must reach logout_user with the refresh token.

The claim that the OTA is the activation lever is therefore wrong, and a backend-only admin.sign_out(access_token, 'local') would revoke for every installed build today. summary:
W2-1 (PR #137) does not hold up. Of the five FOCUS attacks, the double-charge and Serper-probe 403 claims survive; the refund, anon-half and unflagged-repair claims don't, and the probe also fails a second way (429 under an anonymous 403 flood). The good news: no double charge (only the routes consume credits, never the orchestrator), and the probe reads a keyed 200 and a keyless 403 correctly.

Two major defects I reproduced:
- **Camera keeps the credit on a failed comparison.** When compare_from_text returns success:False (TIMEOUT, INSUFFICIENT_DATA, LLM_UNAVAILABLE), the route treats it as a delivery: with the flag ON it keeps the credit, bumps the lifetime counter and writes history. This is a seventh non-delivery exit the PR never counted.
- **The unflagged /url/compare fix exposes a hidden failure, live now.** When the verdict LLM fails, the route returns 200 success:true with a made-up winner_index 0 and passes str(e) to the client (it echoed an 'sk-proj-…' probe string). With the flag ON it also charges the user and writes history. A merged test asserts this behaviour as correct.

Also major, from reading the code: the documented 'sequence after #128 for the anon half' cannot close /url/compare, which has no anonymous gate at all. The camera anon credit is still never refunded.

Minor defects: a credit-burning 500 when the vision model returns size_or_count as a number (reproduced). /url/compare with the flag OFF is not identical: it now runs a token check, which returns 401 under strict auth (reproduced). An anonymous 403 flood pushes the admin prices probe to 429 on one shared bucket (reproduced). The PR's 'no bare-dict mock' claim is false (reproduced: /text/parse returns parsed:'products'). The refunds drop consumed_keys. CLAUDE.md has a stale line reference and two scope items that never shipped.

Mutations: four load-bearing pins SURVIVED (moderation-exception refund, the refund latch, the URL exception refund, the /text/parse unpack). The delivery-refund control was KILLED. The unit's own 30 tests pass on the pinned venv.

Method: detached scratch worktree at origin/main b6f94052, 8+1 probe nodes all reproducing, every mutation restored with a sha256-verified check, worktree removed and confirmed gone from git worktree list.

The finding explicitly left two causes open: RLS never took, or a permissive policy was added out of band. The second-vote reviewer could not tell which (PGRST107). I ran the other branch on the local PG with RLS enabled plus a `USING (true)` SELECT policy. anon saw 4/4 rows before 037, and still saw 4/4 after 037 was applied. activation_gate: No flag; this is an unapplied migration. What 037 claims for its four named functions holds on a real engine. On a throwaway local PostgreSQL 18 cluster with Supabase-style anon/authenticated/service_role(BYPASSRLS) roles and an auth.uid() shim, 036 then 037 gave the right result both with stock default privileges (named anon/authenticated grants) and with the PUBLIC default only. anon and authenticated got 42501 on delete_user_cascade and increment_lifetime_comparisons. service_role still ran both: a real delete cascaded and the lifetime counter went 0 to 1. resolve_referral_code still resolves for anon and service_role. home_savings_aggregate is denied to anon and allowed to authenticated. user_events RLS gives anon 0 rows, the own user 2, and service_role 4, and service_role can INSERT a row with a non-null user_id, so the PR's 'partial failure' scenario does not happen when service_role has BYPASSRLS. Re-applying 037 is idempotent, rollback/025 (CREATE OR REPLACE) keeps the tightened ACL, and every production .rpc( caller uses get_admin_supabase_client (database_service.py:384, usage_service.py:514/706, referral_service.py:398 via :207), with home_savings_aggregate on the user or admin client (home_routes.py:213-216). Applying 037 is therefore SAFE and strictly better than today, and Ahmed may apply it, but it is NOT sufficient. Gate before calling CR-SECURITY-01/02 closed: (1) run the pg_class relrowsecurity query and the pg_policies query for user_events BEFORE applying and keep the output; if RLS is already on or an extra policy exists, 037 will not close CR-SECURITY-02; (2) run the anon-executable SECURITY DEFINER census on the live catalog, which must show cleanup_expired_ratings, and close it in a follow-up 038; (3) 037 currently needs 036 applied first, but it does NOT need 035, whose own header says not to apply it. Either apply 036 then 037, or ship W1-2d's guarded statement 4 and apply 037 alone. (4) After apply: proacl shows no anon, authenticated or bare =X entries on the two service-role functions; the anon-key POST probe returns 42501; anon count=exact on user_events == 0; and an anon GET on rpc/cleanup_expired_ratings no longer returns 25006.
summary: I re-derived PR #153 and ran it on a real engine: a throwaway local PG 18 cluster emulating Supabase roles, with its data dir inside my scratch worktree, both removed afterwards. The reworked grant fix is correct. REVOKE FROM PUBLIC, anon, authenticated plus an explicit GRANT to service_role closes anon and authenticated EXECUTE under both ACL worlds, and every production caller keeps working because they all use the service-role admin client. The user_events ENABLE is idempotent and does not break service-role writes, and a failed apply rolls back completely. The unit is still DEFECTIVE. (1) It declares the live, anon-callable DELETE function cleanup_expired_ratings nonexistent on the strength of a repo grep, and pins that in a test, so CR-SECURITY-01 stays partly open after apply. (2) It assumes CR-SECURITY-02 means 'RLS off'. When the cause is a permissive out-of-band policy, I measured that 037 changes nothing (anon 4/4 rows) and the rollback leaves the table worse than before (RLS disabled, anon can DELETE). (3) It makes '035 -> 036 -> 037' a hard prerequisite, although 037 needs only 036 and 035 says not to apply it, so the security fix is blocked for no technical reason. (4) Five load-bearing mutations survive the 'durable guard', including a later DROP+CREATE that reopens the hole. Unit tests on the pinned venv: 21 passed, 4 skipped. I made no edits or git writes in the shared trees. The scratch worktree was removed and git worktree list confirms it.

defects.claim: The admin key still leaves the building. Every sampled performance TRANSACTION for an authenticated admin request carries the operator's real X-Admin-Key verbatim in request.headers. _before_send is never called for transactions, and the SDK's own header filter does not cover it (SENSITIVE_HEADERS in sentry_sdk/integrations/_wsgi_common.py is authorization/cookie/set-cookie/proxy-authorization/x-api-key/x-forwarded-for/x-real-ip, with no x-admin-key). Measured on sentry-sdk 2.68.1, the pinned version (the venv has it). The Sentry setup went through the REAL init_sentry(), with only the transport and traces_sample_rate=1.0 injected. The app was driven over raw ASGI. Results: GET /api/v1/admin/stats/daily with the correct key gave 200, 1 transaction, key_in_tx=True, leaking header 'x-admin-key'. GET /admin/cohort.html with the correct X-Admin-Key gave 200, key_in_tx=True. Basic auth on the mount did not leak, because the SDK filters Authorization. The result is identical with include_local_variables on or off.
defects.why_it_matters: The PR's headline and its one Ahmed action rest on the leak being closed: rotate ADMIN_API_KEY 'when this deploys'. In prod traces_sample_rate=0.1, so about 1 in 10 calls from cohort/costs/referrals.html (they fetch /api/v1/admin/* with the X-Admin-Key the operator types in) and from curl ships the key to Sentry. A key rotated now leaks again on the first admin-dashboard session. Error events are clean (before_send redacts the header), but transactions are a separate stream, and the unit's tests only ever call _before_send on fixture dicts, so nothing could see this. Server-side Relay scrubbing of an 'x-admin-key' field name is unverified (org settings were not readable here). The default sensitive-field list does not obviously match it.

It also walks spans[].data with _scrub_dict while leaving trace/span ids alone, and it must not run the 503-drop on transactions. Factor the request-region scrub into one helper both hooks call, so the two can't drift. defects.location: app/main.py:401-413 (_AdminAuthenticatedStaticFiles Basic branch; except (binascii.Error, UnicodeDecodeError))
defects.claim: The unauthenticated /admin/* mount still 500s. An Authorization header whose Basic payload holds a raw byte >= 0x80 (b'Basic \xff\xfe') makes base64.b64decode(str) raise a plain ValueError ('string argument should contain only ASCII characters', chained from UnicodeEncodeError). binascii.Error is a SUBCLASS of ValueError, not the reverse, so the except clause misses it, the exception escapes, the app returns 500, and a Sentry error event is captured. Measured over raw ASGI: status 500, 1 error event. With include_local_variables=False (as shipped) the event has no vars and no key. With include_local_variables=True (the primary fix regressed, belt only), the probe found the key in frame __call__ vars 'expected' and 'expected_bytes'. The PR's test sends a base64-encoded non-ASCII password (that correctly gives 401), not a raw non-ASCII header, so the class TestAdminStaticMountNeverReturns500 does not cover this door.
defects.why_it_matters: The PR's 'three doors' claim, and CLAUDE.md's 'both main.py static-mount branches … 403 where 500'd', are false for this input. Any anonymous caller can mint one Sentry error event per request on a mount with no route limit (SlowAPIMiddleware is flag-gated). That burns Sentry quota and pollutes the 5xx rate this campaign uses to read its canaries. It is also a one-regression-away key disclosure, because the belt scrub does not catch 'expected'.
defects.proposed_fix_unit: W1-1c 'mount Basic branch never raises'. File: app/main.py. Change the handler to `except (ValueError, UnicodeError):` (ValueError already covers binascii.Error), or decode the header value to bytes first with base64.b64decode(authz[6:].encode('latin-1')). Either way, any malformed Basic header falls through to the 401 + WWW-Authenticate response. RED test in tests/test_admin_key_and_sentry_scrub.py::TestAdminStaticMountNeverReturns500: client.get('/admin/cohort.html', headers={'Authorization': b'Basic \xff\xfe'}) must give 401. TestClient accepts bytes header values, as the existing X-Admin-Key raw_header parametrisation shows. Add b'Basic \xc3\xa9' as a second parameter. It currently returns 500.

defects.location: app/services/sentry_service.py:91 (_SENSITIVE_KEY_FRAGMENTS) and :165-168 (frame-vars walk)
defects.claim: The frame-vars 'belt' does not scrub the admin key under the local names that actually hold it. The name denylist is api_key/apikey/token/secret/password. It misses expected, expected_bytes, x_admin_key, x_admin and the mount's `headers` dict entries 'x-admin-key'/'authorization'. So the belt removes the key only when its VALUE matches a pattern (lowercase hex of 32+ chars, JWT, sk-proj, fc-). The unit's frame_vars test uses a 64-char lowercase hex key and passes for that reason alone; the test file's own docstring admits this. Measured: with a non-hex key and locals on, 'expected' and 'expected_bytes' reach the outgoing event.
defects.why_it_matters: The primary fix (include_local_variables=False, killed by mutation C) carries all the weight. The PR body presents the walk as a second layer, but for this very secret it is a no-op unless the prod key happens to be lowercase hex. Any future init path, or a test that re-enables locals, puts the key back in events.
defects.proposed_fix_unit: Fold into W1-1b. Add 'admin_key', 'authorization', 'cookie', 'expected' (or better, redact by VALUE: in _before_send, read ADMIN_API_KEY and the other process secrets once and replace any exact occurrence in the serialized strings with '[REDACTED]'). A value-based redaction is shape-independent and closes the name-coverage problem that the PR itself calls unmaintainable. RED test: the existing frame_vars region case, re-run with ADMIN_API_KEY set to a non-hex value and vars {'expected': repr(key), 'headers': {'x-admin-key': key}}, asserting the key is absent after _before_send.

summary: I re-derived the PR #142 claims on the pinned venv (sentry-sdk 2.68.1, fastapi 0.141.1) in a detached scratch worktree, now removed and confirmed gone from git worktree list. The unit file passed 50/50. The claims that hold: verify_admin_key compares bytes and 403s for missing or non-ASCII keys; the three compare_digest sites compare bytes; include_local_variables=False is set and really does remove frame vars; the trace-id restore and the 503-drop are intact. Mutations B, C, D and E were killed. Mutation A survived: the constant-time pins are source greps that the docstring satisfies. The PR's headline, that the admin key stops leaving the building, is false. I drove the real init_sentry() through an in-memory transport. Every sampled performance transaction for an authenticated admin call (both /api/v1/admin/* and the /admin mount via X-Admin-Key) ships the real key in request.headers, because _before_send does not run on transactions and the SDK's own header filter does not list x-admin-key. At the prod sample rate of 0.1, that means the rotation Ahmed was told to do on deploy would leak the new key the first time the admin dashboards are used. Separately, the unauthenticated /admin mount still 500s on a raw non-ASCII Basic header: base64.b64decode raises ValueError, which the binascii.Error handler misses. That 500 produces a Sentry error event per anonymous request, and it would disclose the key if locals were ever turned back on, since the belt scrub does not match 'expected'. Two new units are proposed: W1-1b (before_send_transaction plus a value-based scrub, with an end-to-end envelope test) and W1-1c (catch ValueError on the mount). The key rotation is re-gated behind W1-1b.

defects.location: app/services/auth_service.py::_categorize_auth_error (substring branch, ~:173-188) as used by app/api/auth_routes.py::refresh (the 503 branch)
defects.claim: The transient-class classifier misses most real Supabase outage shapes, so /auth/refresh still returns 401 for them. The route matches substrings of str(e) ('network','connection','timeout','dns',...). I drove auth_service.refresh_session through the real pinned SDK (supabase/supabase_auth 2.31.0, httpx 0.28.1) against a local fake gotrue on 127.0.0.1. Results: upstream 502, 503 (both body shapes), 520, 522, 429 rate limit, 500 unexpected_failure, 544 'Request timed out', a dropped connection (httpx.RemoteProtocolError 'Server disconnected without sending a response.') and a REAL hang hitting the SDK's own ~5 s timeout (message 'timed out', which does not contain the substring 'timeout') ALL map to 401 AUTH_REQUIRED. Only 504 ('Gateway Timeout'), connection refused and connection reset map to 503. Synthetic Linux messages also map to 401: name-resolution failures ('[Errno -3] Temporary failure in name resolution', 'Name or service not known'), ReadTimeout 'The read operation timed out', a TLS handshake timeout, PoolTimeout and SSL EOF. The SDK itself already classifies 502/503/504/520-530 and every non-HTTP transport error as AuthRetryableError, and the categoriser ignores that type. Note that httpx transport errors escape _request unwrapped because it only catches HTTPStatusError and RuntimeError.
defects.why_it_matters: The PR title and the CLAUDE.md row both claim 'stop a Supabase blip logging out the fleet' and 'precondition (1) IS NOW LIVE' for ENABLE_STRICT_OPTIONAL_AUTH. Both are false for the common blip shapes: a timeout, a 502/503 from Supabase's edge or a dropped connection. The pre-OTA client (97b5f15, authService.refreshSession) calls clearSession() on any 401 from /auth/refresh, and so does the post-OTA client (sessionInvalid, then emitSessionInvalid, which force-routes to Auth). So a real outage still logs users out. Supabase's per-IP refresh rate limit is shared by the whole fleet because every refresh comes from the Railway IP. Its 429 is also mapped to 401, which turns one rate-limit burst into mass logouts. Any flag flip or OTA gated on 'precondition (1)' is gated on a false fact.
defects.proposed_fix_unit: W1-4b 'classify refresh failures by type, not by substring'. Keep 401 for AuthApiError with status 400/401/403/404 and for codes like refresh_token_not_found, refresh_token_already_used and session_not_found. Keep the existing substring branch as a fallback. Red test in tests/test_auth_refresh_and_revocation.py: replace node 1's synthetic ConnectionError('connection timeout') with a parametrised table of REAL exception objects built through the SDK. Either run a local ThreadingHTTPServer on 127.0.0.1 that answers /auth/v1/token with 429/500/502/503/504/520/522, closes the socket, or sleeps past the timeout, or construct supabase_auth.helpers.handle_exception(httpx.HTTPStatusError(...)) plus httpx.ReadTimeout('timed out') and httpx.ConnectError('[Errno -3] Temporary failure in name resolution'). defects.location: app/services/auth_service.py::get_auth_client / refresh_session / logout_user (flag-ON path); supabase_auth/_sync/gotrue_client.py::_save_session → _start_auto_refresh_token (auto_refresh_token defaults to True)
defects.claim: Every successful server-side refresh leaves an orphaned SDK auto-refresh timer, and that timer later spends the refresh token the device was just given. This predates W1-4 and is outside its diff, but it sits on the same path. get_auth_client() builds a throw-away anon client with default options (auto_refresh_token=True). client.auth.refresh_session() therefore calls _save_session, which starts a daemon Timer for (expires_in - 10 s). When it fires, _call_refresh_token runs with the session's refresh token and re-arms itself, forever, for the life of the process. Measured locally with a 12 s expiry: after one POST /auth/refresh returned RT-1 to the 'device', the server made 18 unsolicited POST /auth/v1/token calls in 9 s with no request in flight. The first of them presented RT-1, the device's token. With a 3600 s expiry the first timer fires about 59m50s after each refresh. I measured the same leak on the flag-ON logout path. When sign_out succeeds the timer is cancelled (_remove_session). When the sign_out leg fails (here: dropped connection, RemoteProtocolError), the timer set up by set_session survives. The server then keeps refreshing the session the user just logged out of, while logout_user reports success.
defects.why_it_matters: The client code's own model (api.ts P-A3 comment) says that presenting an already-spent refresh token outside the 10 s reuse window revokes the whole session family. The server spends each device's token about 10 s before its access token expires, and then keeps advancing the chain every hour. A device that comes back after the chain has moved on presents a spent token, gets 401 on refresh, and is logged out. GoTrue's parent-of-active allowance may forgive a single hop; that is UNVERIFIED here, as no live test was run. On top of that, the number of timer chains and the upstream refresh traffic from the Railway IP grow with every login and refresh until the next deploy. That traffic feeds the per-IP rate limit, whose 429 the classifier above maps to 401. Deploys reset the chains, which likely hides the problem.
defects.proposed_fix_unit: W1-4c 'server-side Supabase clients must never auto-refresh'. File app/services/auth_service.py: build the anon client with ClientOptions(auto_refresh_token=False, persist_session=False) on both branches of get_auth_client, merging into build_supabase_client_options() when the shared-transport flag is on. Check that login, social login, refresh and logout do not depend on the timer. In logout_user, add a finally that calls client.auth._remove_session() (or sign_out with suppression) so a failed sign_out leg cannot leave a stored session behind. Red test: a local 127.0.0.1 fake gotrue returning expires_in=12. Call auth_service.refresh_session, sleep about 4 s, and assert exactly ONE POST /auth/v1/token. Today it records about 18. A second test: flag ON, the fake closes the socket on /auth/v1/logout; assert no live supabase_auth Timer remains after logout_user returns. Decide whether this needs a flag. It changes no response bytes, so it can probably ship unflagged.

activation_gate: The REFRESH half is UNFLAGGED and LIVE. It is safe, in the sense that it only turns some 401s into 503s. The pre-OTA 97b5f15 client handles a 503 gracefully: refreshSession returns success:false without clearSession, performRefresh returns the stale token, the original request is retried once, gets 401 and is rejected, and initializeAuth returns the cached user. There is no logout and no loop. The post-OTA client also treats a non-401 as transient and does not emit sessionInvalid. But the fix covers only 504, connection refused and connection reset. Timeouts, 502/503/52x, 429, 500 and dropped connections still return 401, and 401 means forced logout on both client versions. So ENABLE_STRICT_OPTIONAL_AUTH precondition (1) is NOT satisfied, and the CLAUDE.md 'IS NOW LIVE' line must be corrected. Gate that flag, and any OTA justified by 'the backend refresh fix is live', on W1-4b landing, with its real-SDK-exception table green. Gate it also on W1-4c: the orphaned auto-refresh timer that spends device refresh tokens server-side. The LOGOUT half, ENABLE_LOGOUT_UPSTREAM_REVOCATION (default OFF, read per call), is byte-identical when OFF: node 6 pins exactly one bare sign_out() and the same body, and M8 (flag forced on) turns node 6 red. When ON it stays inert for every build without PR #140's client half, and scope 'local' is pinned (M4 is killed by nodes 3 and 4). Before flipping it: land W1-4c (so a failed sign_out leg cannot leave a perpetual refresh chain for a logged-out session) and the two scrub pins, then canary on the count of '[auth] logout upstream leg failed' WARNINGs. It only takes effect once the PR #140 OTA is on phones.

Verdict: DEFECTIVE. The refresh half is live and harmless to both client versions, but it does not do what the PR and CLAUDE.md say. On origin/main b203cfcc (auth functions unchanged since merge 98f320fb), all 7 unit tests pass on the pinned venv (.venv-qaren: fastapi 0.141.1, supabase 2.31.0).

**Mutation checks (10 run):** 8 were killed: dropping the 503 branch, a bare 503, dropping the marker, sign_out without options, skipping set_session, dropping the scrub, forcing the flag on, and mapping every failure to 503. 2 survived: a raw `{e}` in the route backstop, and dropping refresh-token redaction.

**Blocking defect:** I drove the real SDK against a local fake gotrue. A real timeout ('timed out'), upstream 502/503/520/522, a 429, a 500 and a dropped connection all still return 401. The classifier matches substrings and ignores the SDK's own AuthRetryableError and httpx.TransportError types. Only 504, connection refused and connection reset get the 503. So 'a Supabase blip no longer logs out the fleet' and 'ENABLE_STRICT_OPTIONAL_AUTH precondition (1) IS NOW LIVE' are both false. Node 1 passes only because its input is a synthetic ConnectionError('connection timeout') written to contain the substrings.

It spends the device's refresh token about 10 s before the access token expires, and keeps going for the life of the process (18 unsolicited token POSTs in 9 s with a 12 s expiry). - The logout body parameter now returns 422 for non-JSON bodies and skips the blacklist write. No shipped client sends such a body.
- Two scrub rules have no test.

**Pre-OTA client (97b5f15) on a 503:** no sign-out and no loop. It retries once with the stale token and returns the cached user at boot.

**Logout flag (ENABLE_LOGOUT_UPSTREAM_REVOCATION):** byte-identical when OFF (pinned, and the mutation that forces it on turns that pin red). When ON it is inert until the PR #140 OTA is on phones.

defects.location: app/services/database_service.py:138-150 (get_shared_httpx_client: one httpx.Client(http2=True) shared by every Supabase client); interaction with httpcore 1.0.9 _sync/http2.py:342-460
defects.claim: The 8 s knob does not bound a hung PostgREST call, and one hung call on the shared HTTP/2 connection stalls or kills unrelated requests. httpcore's HTTP/2 read timeout applies to each socket read made by whichever thread currently holds the connection's read lock, not to each request. Result 1: under concurrent traffic the read keeps getting data, so a hung stream is never timed out. Measured with read=2 s and 4 concurrent workers: the hung call ended at 7.95 s, 2 s after the traffic stopped; on its own connection it ended at 2.00 s. Result 2: under sparse traffic the hung stream holds the read lock, so other requests are starved until its read times out. That read then records _read_exception for the whole connection. A 400 ms request issued 1.8 s into a hung call failed with ReadTimeout after 0.2 s; the same request succeeded in 0.44 s on its own connection. In a second run a 0 ms request took 2.0 s.
defects.why_it_matters: The CLAUDE.md flag row and PR body say the flag bounds every PostgREST session at 8 s. With the flag ON that is false under load, and every authed request is coupled to the slowest in-flight Supabase call: user-scoped, anon/auth and both admin clients share one connection. In the collateral case, writes such as save_comparison or usage increments can commit on the server while the client sees a ReadTimeout. Base already has this coupling, but only among admin calls on the memoised database_service admin client, with a 120 s window. The flag spreads it to all Supabase traffic and makes it fire far more often. /home/savings, which already runs longer than 8 s, is the likely trigger. Inference, not measured, because the network was off-limits: Supabase negotiates h2 over ALPN (h2==4.4.1 is pinned in requirements.txt).
defects.proposed_fix_unit: W0-2b: build the shared transport with http2=False, which gives an HTTP/1.1 keep-alive pool with one request per connection. This keeps the whole CR-PERFORMANCE-03 win, because the saved ~215 ms is SSLContext/certifi setup and not the connection, and it removes cross-request head-of-line blocking and connection-wide timeout poisoning. Size the limits so max_connections is at least the run_db executor width (40) plus headroom. Red tests in tests/test_supabase_client_reuse.py: (a) start a loopback h2c/h1 server that never answers /hang and answers /fast at once. Through get_shared_httpx_client(), run /hang while 4 threads loop /fast, and assert /hang raises within knob+0.5 s. Today it runs 7.95 s against a 2 s knob. (b) Issue a 400 ms request 1.8 s into /hang and assert it succeeds. Today it raises ReadTimeout. For TLS parity with prod, assert shared._transport._pool._http2 is False. Repro script: scratchpad/repro/h2_shared_timeout.py and exp3.py. Keep the flag OFF until this lands.

defects.location: app/utils/url_validator.py:358-368 (started-timeout memo) and :382-386 / :269-273 (gaierror memo)
defects.claim: The 60 s negative memo still blacklists healthy hosts in three ways that the queued-vs-started fix does not cover. (A) A transient gaierror is memoised: EAI_AGAIN (resolver SERVFAIL) blocks the host for 60 s. Flag OFF gives 1st=False, 2nd=True. Flag ON gives 1st=False, 2nd=False, sync3rd=False, with 1 resolve. (B) A slow but healthy host is memoised: a 2.4 s resolve that succeeds becomes a 60 s block even after the zombie thread has returned a public address. Flag OFF: True after 2.41 s, then True. Flag ON: False at 2.00 s, then False with no second resolve. (C) started.is_set() does not mean the host is slow. A job that waited in the queue and got a worker just before the deadline is memoised after only milliseconds of resolving. Measured at the default pool of 16: 16 black-holed hosts plus 1 healthy store with a 0.35 s cold resolve gave healthy 1st=False, and 1.5 s later with the pool idle and the resolver instant it was still False from the memo. The 8-of-8 poisoning the orchestrator fixed still exists at the pool's edge.
defects.why_it_matters: The memo is per process and shared by all users. One resolver hiccup or one saturation burst takes a legitimate storefront off the price path and the /url/* routes for 60 s, where base retries on the next call. The saturation burst is attacker-reachable through unauthenticated /url/* with random black-holed subdomains. This is the same failure class the orchestrator's fix was meant to close. CLAUDE.md names only the slow-host case as a canary-watch and calls that host black-holed, which (B) shows it may not be.
defects.proposed_fix_unit: W0-1b in app/utils/url_validator.py. (1) Memoise a gaierror only for EAI_NONAME, and EAI_NODATA where the platform defines it. EAI_AGAIN and other codes fail closed for this call only. (2) Record time.monotonic() inside _resolve when it starts. Memoise a timeout only when (deadline - start) >= 0.75 * timeout, so the resolve really ran for most of the bound. (3) Add a done-callback on the concurrent future: when the zombie later returns a public address, _memo_pop(hostname). A negative memo is never kept after proof that the host resolves. Red tests in tests/test_url_validator_offloop.py: (A) a stub raising gaierror(EAI_AGAIN) once then public, and assert the 2nd call is True. (B) A stub sleeping timeout+0.4 then returning public, then an instant stub, and assert the 2nd call after the zombie returns is True. (C) Pool 1 with a blocker released at 0.9*timeout and a healthy stub taking 0.2*timeout, and assert the memo is None afterwards. Keep test_started_timeout_is_memoized green; a stub that runs the full bound is still memoised. Repro: scratchpad/repro/dns_repro.py sections A-C.

defects.location: app/utils/url_validator.py:338-381 (no in-flight coalescing)
defects.claim: There is no single-flight per hostname. N concurrent validations of the same black-holed host each take a pool worker, because the memo is written only after the timeout. Measured: 16 concurrent validations of one host occupied all 16 workers, and an unrelated healthy store was rejected after 2.00 s (queued past the bound, not memoised).
defects.why_it_matters: The bounded pool is the whole design, and 16 requests to one attacker hostname fill it for the OS resolver timeout (11-12 s in prod), so every other /url/* and price-path validation fails closed. The price fan-out also sends many URLs on one host concurrently, so one slow storefront fills the pool by itself. Flag ON is still much better than base, which freezes the loop, but the claim that the pool bounds the blast radius holds only for zombies, not for denial of the validator.
defects.proposed_fix_unit: W0-1c: keep a dict hostname -> asyncio.Future of in-flight resolves on the loop. Later callers await the existing future, shielded and with their own wait_for, instead of submitting a new job. Optionally cap concurrent resolves per registrable domain (for example 2) so random-subdomain floods of one attacker domain cannot fill all 16 workers. Red test: 16 concurrent validate_external_url_async calls for one host, with a stub that blocks until released, assert getaddrinfo is called once. Then a healthy host validated during that period returns True. Repro: scratchpad/repro/dns_repro.py section D.

defects.claim: One compare can trip the global openai breaker while OpenAI is healthy. Every in-flight guarded dispatch that an outer wall cancels records its own failure. So a single deadline event that cancels 3 or more concurrent LLM calls reaches CB_FAILURE_THRESHOLD in one burst. The breaker then goes OPEN for CB_RECOVERY_TIMEOUT (600 s), and the preflight refuses every compare from every user. The PR body's 'three *consecutive* records' bound is refuted, as is the wave-plan contract 'three consecutive 429s'. The breaker counts cancellations, not OpenAI failures. Tier-2 alone fans out one search plus one gpt call per missing non-negotiable field (smartphone: battery, processor, ram, rear_camera = 4), for both products at once.
defects.why_it_matters: When the flag is flipped, a slow scrape plus normal LLM latency can refuse all compares for 10 minutes ('Still warming up the comparison engine'). No 429 or 5xx is needed. After the cooldown the next compare that hits a wall can re-trip it. Flag ON can then be worse than flag OFF on a healthy OpenAI: it turns ordinary per-compare timeouts into a global outage. With Serper dead in prod, every Tier-2 search goes to Bright Data, whose 2-5 s latency puts the LLM calls in flight right at the 4 s wall. The merged test test_wait_for_timeout_around_the_guard_records_a_failure pins the behaviour that causes this.
defects.proposed_fix_unit: W1-3a 'cancellation is not an OpenAI health signal'. Files: app/services/api_budget_service.py (guarded_llm_create) and tests/test_openai_breaker.py. Change: stop recording a failure on a bare CancelledError. A cancel from a sibling's wall, the hard cap, a disconnect or shutdown says nothing about OpenAI. Capture genuine OpenAI stalls another way: either rely on the SDK's own request timeout (APITimeoutError is an APIConnectionError, already classified transient), or give guarded_llm_create an optional `deadline` kwarg enforced by `asyncio.timeout()` inside the guard, so only the guard's own TimeoutError is recorded. Also dedupe to at most one recorded failure per compare, using a contextvar set at the two compare entries, so one request can never reach the threshold alone. Rewrite the MINOR-5 test: an external cancellation must be re-raised and must NOT record. RED test (runs in about 0.3 s): flag ON, dict-stubbed breaker Redis, monkeypatch scs._TIER2_WALL_SECONDS=0.3, stub serper_service.search_web to return one snippet, and point openai_service.get_client at a client whose create sleeps 5 s. defects.claim: The half-open probe can wedge the breaker into deny-all while the preflight admits every compare. Setup: a cooldown-expired OPEN breaker whose probe dispatch fails with a non-transient error, such as a 400 context-length or content-policy rejection, 401/403/404/422, or any non-SDK exception. Nothing is recorded. The probe budget (INCR = 1) is spent and the blob stays half_open. Every later dispatch INCRs to 2 or more and raises LLMUnavailableError, even with OpenAI healthy. The preflight reads half_open and returns True, so every compare still pays the full Serper/Bright Data/Firecrawl fan-out before its LLM calls are denied. Nothing clears this until the blob's _CB_TTL (3600 s) lapses, because denied checks never write. Killing the probe's process mid-call (SIGKILL/OOM, no CancelledError) has the same effect.
defects.why_it_matters: For up to one hour, flag ON is strictly worse than flag OFF: 100% compare failure on a healthy OpenAI, while still paying the whole scrape cost the unit exists to save. The PR's 'no permanent lockout' fix covered only the preflight side; the dispatch-side probe can still be orphaned. The claim that the probe 'is spent at a real dispatch that records an outcome' is false for every non-transient outcome.
defects.proposed_fix_unit: W1-3b 'every admitted half-open probe records an outcome'. File: app/services/api_budget_service.py guarded_llm_create/_openai_dispatch_admission. Change: when outcome_matters is True (a half-open admission), make the outcome total. An openai.APIStatusError with 4xx other than 429 means the server answered, so record it as liveness (openai_record_success); any other non-transient exception calls openai_record_failure, which re-opens the breaker for a fresh window instead of wedging it. As defence in depth, have is_circuit_closed re-admit a new probe when half_open_calls has been spent for longer than a stale-probe window (for example 2x the OpenAI request timeout). Optionally, have the preflight deny while a half-open probe is outstanding, reading the probe counter with a plain GET and never an INCR, so concurrent compares do not pay the fan-out just to be denied. RED test: seed OPEN with tripped_at = now - (CB_RECOVERY_TIMEOUT+5), then run guarded_llm_create with a client raising openai.BadRequestError (status 400). Then run 10 iterations, each resetting the memo and calling guarded_llm_create with a healthy client, and assert at least one dispatch reaches the client and the blob is not half_open. On main it is RED: 10 of 10 LLMUnavailableError, 0 healthy dispatches, preflight admitted 10 of 10, blob {'state':'half_open','half_open_calls':1}. Probe: scratchpad/w13adv/test_zz_w13_adversary_probe.py::test_P2.

Three non-consecutive failures, with any number of successes in between, therefore trip the breaker. defects.why_it_matters: The breaker becomes a failure counter with no decay rather than a consecutive-failure detector. It trips more easily than documented, so the flag flip is less predictable. Bounded: a trip lasts 10 minutes.

summary:
PR #147 is DEFECTIVE, but only for the flag flip; nothing live today is affected because the flag is OFF. The flag-OFF path and the preflight-side lockout fixes hold. The shipped snapshot design has a blocking defect and a major one that the rework introduced or left, and both reproduced in a scratch worktree at origin/main 2ec8131e on the pinned venv.

**What I confirmed:**
- All 18 of the unit's tests pass.
- The CLAUDE.md line references (:709/:712/:1520/:3325/:3964/:811) and the count of 14 call sites (8+4+1+1) are accurate.
- The streaming preflight sits after the six counter resets and before the L1 prefilter, as claimed.
- Neither preflight lockout the rework named comes back: the preflight is read-only, uses no `is_circuit_closed`, and a cooldown-expired OPEN is let through so the dispatch can move it to half-open.
- 13 mutations on CRLF-exact source, each restored from a byte snapshot with a matching sha256: 11 turned the tests red and 2 survived (the M6 transient classifier and the M10 flag-OFF entry read). An earlier run also turned M8 (503 mapping) and M13 (memo TTL) red.

**Blocking:** the rework that makes the guard record a failure on every cancellation means one compare can trip the global breaker while OpenAI is healthy. Driving the real `tier2_fill_non_negotiables` with the wall shortened to 0.3 s and slow but healthy LLM calls, a single compare left the breaker `{'state':'open','failure_count':4}`. The preflight then refused every compare for 600 s. The 4 s Tier-2 wall, the 25 s hard caps and the per-stage `wait_for`s all do this.

**Major:** a half-open probe that ends in a non-transient error, or an orphaned probe, wedges the breaker. Every dispatch is denied for up to the 3600 s blob TTL, while the preflight still admits every compare, so each one pays the full scrape fan-out and then fails. Measured: 10 of 10 dispatches denied, 0 reached a healthy client, 10 of 10 compares admitted.

**Minor:**
- A success seen by another worker never resets the shared failure count, so 3 non-consecutive failures still trip it.
- The M6 and M10 behaviours are unpinned by any test.
- The PR's corpus byte-identity SHA is vacuous for this unit: that harness only runs `price_service.extract_price_from_html`, which the PR does not change.

The scratch worktree is removed and `git worktree list` confirms it. The probe tests and the mutation driver and results are saved under the scratchpad folder w13adv/.

summary:
I found no correctness defect in what W0-4 changes, but the unit is incomplete against its own wave-plan row, and the CLAUDE.md activation text makes claims that are false or were never proven.

**What holds:**
- **Parse once:** one BeautifulSoup per call under the flag (5888 -> 1656 over the corpus).
- **Read-only soup:** the shared soup is only read by the JSON-LD passes. The one mutating branch (WooCommerce) runs after them.
- **Exceptions:** an exception inside the worker thread is re-raised on the loop (measured).
- **ContextVar:** asyncio.to_thread copies it, so the resolved category reaches the parse (0/828 different on the async leg).
- **No memo collision:** there is no cross-call memo keyed by an HTML hash. The soup lives in one call frame, so the collision the focus asked about cannot happen.
- **Flag OFF:** byte-identical. The recorded base 9504e5a9... reproduces on current main.
- **Flag ON:** result-identical to OFF on the whole frozen corpus (results sha a1b3460c... both sides). The harness cannot run flag ON, so I measured this myself; nobody had.

**What is wrong:**
- **Memory cap missing (major):** the 3 MB fetch cap the row required was never built. curl_fetch_html and the firecrawl/scrapedo render legs stay uncapped.
- **Shared pool, no promised cap (major):** the offload uses the shared 40-worker default pool, already measured as oversubscribed by one compare, and the prefetch concurrency cap the flip was supposed to go with does not exist. A cancelled await leaves a zombie parse (measured: timed out at 0.07 s, finished at 0.33 s).
- **False iHerb claim, parse sites left on the loop (major):** CLAUDE.md says fetch_iherb_price already parses off the loop. It does not: only the fetch is offloaded. Bolo, boutiqaat, pharmacy JSON-LD and url_extraction also still parse on the loop.
- **Weak off-loop evidence (minor):** the heartbeat tests use a GIL-releasing sleep stub. Real offloaded parses of large pages still produced 69-633 ms loop gaps on a noisy dev box.
- **Weak ON-identity pin (minor):** the flag-ON identity test covers one synthetic page and survived a mutation that switches the parser only when the flag is ON.

**Method:** all work was in a detached scratch worktree of origin/main b6f94052, and the _proof corpus was read-only. The scratch worktree was removed with git worktree remove --force and confirmed gone in git worktree list. The logs are in C:/Users/SYNACK~1/AppData/Local/Temp/claude/C--Users-SynAckITPC-Documents-AI/a47353ce-a0e3-4273-b85d-f21cfa01e031/scratchpad/w04drv/ (onoff_default.log, gil.log, gil2.log, gil2b.log, mut.log, mut2.log, unit.log), and the official gate output is in scratchpad/gate_main_off.log.
